# What’s Behind the Sharp Drop in Labor Force Participation?

August 04, 2026

By [Alexander Bick](#authorbox)
key_claim: The largest single component of the 2026 fall in the US labour force participation rate, 43 percent, traces to the January 2026 population-control revision rather than to worker behaviour; ongoing ageing accounts for 16 percent and within-group participation for 41 percent.
frame_summary: Bick argues that a headline labour-supply statistic can move sharply for reasons that have nothing to do with workers' decisions, and that decomposing the move into measurement, composition and behaviour is a precondition for reading it at all.
verbatim_quote: The largest single piece of the drop, 43%, traces to one statistical event: the unusually large population-control revision the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) introduced in January 2026.
verbatim_list: The January updates of 2023 through 2025 moved the 65-and-older share by at most 0.14 percentage points, but the January 2026 update raised it by 0.62 percentage points.
The U.S. labor force participation rate—the share of the population age 16 and older working or looking for work—fell to 61.6% in June 2026.
Excluding the 2020-21 period, when the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the labor market, the rate now stands at its lowest level since 1976.

The January revision contributes −0.35 percentage points (43% of the overall decline, the largest single component), ongoing aging accounts for −0.14 percentage points (16%), and within-group participation rates contributes −0.33 percentage points (41%).
notes: Anchor for the measurement-versus-behaviour decomposition. title: Break-even employment declines as unauthorized immigration outflows continue
date_evidence:
# Break-even employment declines as unauthorized immigration outflows continue

Anton Cheremukhin, Daniel Wilson and Xiaoqing Zhou

March 31, 2026
key_claim: US break-even employment growth peaked near 250,000 jobs a month in 2023, fell to roughly 10,000 by July 2025 and averaged about minus 3,000 a month from August to December 2025; net unauthorised immigration averaged minus 55,000 a month in the second half of 2025 and totalled minus 548,000 for the year.
frame_summary: Cheremukhin, Wilson and Zhou argue that the benchmark for judging payroll growth has moved so far that payroll gains which would once have signalled slack are now consistent with a balanced labour market, and that interpreting the data requires importing timely immigration measures.
verbatim_quote: The break-even rate peaked at about 250,000 jobs per month in 2023, fell to roughly 10,000 by July 2025, and declined to near zero thereafter, averaging about –3,000 jobs per month from August to December 2025, indicating, if anything, a modest net jobs loss over this period.
verbatim_list: Our updated estimates indicate that net unauthorized immigration has remained negative since February, averaging -55,000 per month in the second half of 2025

Despite the recent stabilization, total net unauthorized immigration for 2025 reached -548,000, about 50 percent larger in magnitude than the Congressional Budget Office’s [latest projection](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/61879) of -365,000.
As net outflows of unauthorized immigrants reduced employment growth in late 2025, payroll gains that might historically have signaled economic slack are now consistent with a balanced labor market.

title: The latest data shows us that the UK labour market wasn't in good shape on the eve of the Iran war
key_claim: The single-month LFS unemployment estimate swung from 5.2 per cent in December to 4.6 per cent in February and back to 5.5 per cent in March 2026, prompting the Resolution Foundation to caution that LFS estimates should be taken with a pinch of salt; its own employment-rate series rests on tax data and ONS population estimates and carries explicit uncertainty about the pace of population growth.
frame_summary: Cominetti argues that the UK's survey-based headline indicators are too volatile to turn on their own, and that analysts have had to rebuild employment measures from administrative data plus population estimates, importing the population uncertainty as they do so.
verbatim_quote: A useful reminder to take LFS estimates with a pinch of salt.
verbatim_list: The single month estimate was 5.2 per cent in December and fell in both January (to 4.9 January) and February (to 4.6 per cent).
The single-month estimate for March was 5.5 per cent (the highest since 2015), giving a three-month headline figure of 5.0 per cent for Q1 2026.
A caveat to the RF estimates is that there is uncertainty about the current pace of population growth – especially in the migration numbers.

title: Labor Market Recap July 2026
key_claim: US non-farm payrolls fell by 23,000 in July 2026 with May revised down 66,000 and June down 37,000, while the unemployment rate fell 0.10 percentage points to 4.10 per cent; Employ America reads the labour market as stable and notes the breakeven target has been moving for some time.
frame_summary: Mui argues that a negative payroll print and heavy downward revisions no longer amount to labour-market deterioration once the moving breakeven and the survey's own construction are accounted for, and that the Fed should be read as unmoved by them.
verbatim_quote: The unemployment rate fell by 0.10pp in July, while non-farm payrolls fell by 23,000 jobs and May and June payrolls were significantly revised down.
verbatim_list: May’s growth was revised down by 66,000 and June’s was revised down by 37,000.
Perhaps payrolls growth is not as strong as previously thought, but the breakeven payrolls growth target has been a moving target for a while.
The unemployment rate fell another 0.10pp to 4.10%.
In June, the change in the prime-age employment rate was almost all due to differences in the outgoing households versus the incoming households.

title: The labor market could become so backward that the economy will have to shed jobs to keep unemployment steady
key_claim: Oxford Economics estimates the US breakeven rate at about 50,000 jobs a month, down from more than 200,000 in 2022 and 2023, and projects it falling to zero in 2027 and slightly negative in 2028, with employers previously treating 125,000 to 150,000 as the threshold.
frame_summary: Ma argues that the practical meaning of a healthy jobs report is being redefined, and that market and Fed reaction functions keyed to the old payroll thresholds will misfire on the new arithmetic.
verbatim_quote: On Thursday, Oxford Economics estimated the breakeven rate is currently about 50,000 new jobs per month, down from more than 200,000 in 2022 and 2023, when immigration surged.
verbatim_list: For years, monthly job gains of around 125,000 to 150,000 were considered necessary to offset entrants into the workforce.
As a result, the breakeven rate will fall to zero next year and turn slightly negative in 2028, according to economists Matthew Martin and Bernard Yaros.
